metadata.title: PISA 2022 Results Volume III: Creative Minds, Creative Schools Factsheets Brazil

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: This factsheet reports PISA 2022 creative thinking results for Brazil and selected comparison countries/economies, based on the OECD PISA 2022 Database. The text indicates that estimates are presented with uncertainty (95% confidence intervals) and that comparisons are made internationally, which is consistent with PISA’s complex sampling design, but it does not specify the exact student weight variable (e.g., W_FSTUWT) or replicate-weight method (e.g., BRR/jackknife) in the provided excerpt. The factsheet does not describe any ML model fitting or weight-aware estimation steps; therefore, the weighting strategy is not operationalized here beyond the OECD’s standard PISA estimation procedures. No additional preprocessing (e.g., outlier trimming) is described in the excerpt.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: The provided factsheet excerpt reports descriptive and correlational summaries (e.g., mean scores, proficiency shares, and associations with mathematics/reading) rather than detailing an analysis pipeline that uses PISA plausible values (PVs) for a student-level predictive model. Because the excerpt does not specify whether PVs were used directly in any statistical model, PV handling cannot be verified from the text. Missing-data handling is also not described in the excerpt, so the appropriate strategy cannot be assessed from the provided material.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: The excerpt states that, in Brazil, 10,798 students in 599 schools completed the assessment in mathematics, reading or science, representing about 22,630,000 15-year-olds (estimated 76% of the total population of 15-year-olds). No further inclusion/exclusion criteria (e.g., creative-thinking module completion, item-level completion thresholds, or missing-data exclusions) are specified in the provided text.

data.outcome_summary: This OECD PISA 2022 Volume III factsheet summarizes how 15-year-old students in Brazil perform on the PISA Creative Thinking cognitive test, which measures the ability to generate, evaluate, and improve ideas across three ideation processes (generating diverse ideas, generating creative ideas, evaluating and improving ideas) and four domain contexts (written expression, visual expression, social problem solving, scientific problem solving). Brazil’s mean creative thinking score is 23 on a 60-point scale, significantly below the OECD average of 33. The factsheet reports that 46% of students reach at least Level 3 (baseline proficiency), compared with 78% on average across OECD countries, and that 11% are top performers (Levels 5–6), compared with 27% on average. It also reports within-Brazil associations: creative thinking correlates 0.69 with mathematics and 0.7 with reading, and 28% of the variation in creative thinking is uniquely explained by mathematics performance. The excerpt does not provide an ML modeling approach, PV/missing-data procedures, or weighting variable names, so the results should be interpreted as OECD descriptive/benchmark statistics rather than as outputs from a predictive ML study.
data.null_fields_interpretation: This is a descriptive OECD PISA factsheet rather than an empirical ML paper. The excerpt does not report any student-level predictive modeling, algorithm comparisons, or explicit PV/missing-data handling procedures, and it provides only benchmark-style results (means, proficiency levels, and correlations/variance decomposition). As a result, ML technique fields and structured predictive findings are intentionally left empty.
